rows: Distinguish label selection (`.loc`), positional selection (`.iloc`), column selection, and chained indexing.
Use `.loc`/`.iloc` for writes; chained indexing can be ambiguous under copy/view behavior.
Decide whether the result should shrink (`agg`), preserve shape (`transform`), or run arbitrary per-group logic (`apply`).
`apply` is flexible but often slow and harder to reason about than vectorized aggregation.
Identify wide vs long form, uniqueness of index/column pairs, duplicate handling, and whether aggregation is needed.
Check key cardinality, null keys, join type, duplicate keys, index-vs-column joins, and expected row count.
Most surprising Pandas joins are cardinality explosions, not syntax mistakes.
Inspect row count, dtype choices, object columns, vectorization, file format, memory footprint, and whether Polars/DuckDB fits better.
Parquet is usually better for analytics, but CSV may still be right for human exchange or interoperability.
Verify datetime parsing, timezone, index frequency, resampling interval, rolling window semantics, and missing periods.
Timezone and closed/open interval defaults can silently shift results.
